# Glossary {.unnumbered}

Statistical and computational terminology used in this report. Where a term has multiple closely related meanings in the broader literature, the definition below describes the meaning intended in this report specifically.

## Modelling

**Beta-Binomial distribution.** A distribution over bounded counts $y \in \{0, \ldots, N\}$ in which the success probability of each Bernoulli trial is itself drawn from a $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ distribution. Used throughout this report as the likelihood for word counts because it accommodates between-child heterogeneity that a binomial distribution cannot.

**Concentration parameter ($\kappa$).** In our Beta-Binomial parameterisation, $\alpha = p\kappa$ and $\beta = (1 - p)\kappa$. Larger $\kappa$ means less dispersion (the distribution concentrates around its mean $p$); smaller $\kappa$ means more dispersion. We let $\kappa$ vary with age so that residual dispersion can grow as children diverge.

**Dispersion.** A measure of how variable a distribution is around its mean. For the Beta-Binomial likelihood, larger dispersion corresponds to smaller $\kappa$.

**Gaussian process (GP).** A distribution over functions in which every finite set of function values has a joint Gaussian distribution. We use a zero-mean GP with an RBF kernel to model smooth, nonlinear departures from a linear baseline trend on the logit scale of each outcome.

**Hilbert-space Gaussian process (HSGP).** A scalable approximation to an exact GP via a truncated basis expansion, parameterised by basis size $M$ and boundary $c$. Used throughout to make MCMC inference computationally feasible.

**Length-scale ($\ell$).** The GP kernel hyperparameter that controls how rapidly the function varies with age. Short length-scales produce wiggly trajectories; long length-scales produce smooth ones. We constrain $\ell$ to map onto a 6–18-month range so that the GP cannot fit very short-range departures that would over-react to local data composition.

**Amplitude ($\eta$).** The standard deviation of the GP, controlling how large the smooth departures from the linear trend can be on the logit scale.

**Logit.** $\mathrm{logit}(p) = \log(p/(1 - p))$ — the log-odds. Our latent mean trajectories are modelled on the logit scale and transformed back to probabilities through the logistic function $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$.

**Production ratio ($q$).** In the joint models (VG05–VG09), $q = p_S / p_U$ is the fraction of words a child understands that they also produce. Modelled on a separate logit scale so that $p_S = p_U \cdot q$ is enforced by construction.

**Random intercept.** A group-specific offset on the logit scale of an outcome, drawn from a Normal distribution with an unknown SD ($\tau$). The model marginalises over the random intercepts when generating predictions for an unseen group member; for the existing groups it conditions on the posterior estimates.

**Study random intercept.** Added in VG07; one offset per contributing study, absorbing systematic between-study differences in measurement and reporting.

**Subject random intercept.** Added in VG08 (on understood) and VG09 (on understood and on $q$); one offset per unique subject, absorbing the within-subject correlation produced by repeated measures.

**Non-centred parameterisation.** A reparameterisation in which a random effect $\delta = \tau \cdot z$ with $z \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1)$ — decoupling the scale $\tau$ from the unit-scale draws. Used for the subject random intercepts in VG08/VG09 because it produces dramatically better sampling geometry than the centred form when $\tau$ is moderate or large.

**Variance partition.** The decomposition of total observed variability into structural sources (between-study, between-subject, within-occasion dispersion). VG07 partitions out between-study; VG08 partitions out between-subject on understood; VG09 partitions out between-subject on the production ratio. See the [model comparison chapter](model-comparison.qmd) for the headline table.

## Inference

**Prior.** A probability distribution over a parameter that expresses what is plausible *before* looking at the current data. Priors in this report are weakly informative — they encode broad sanity constraints but allow the data to do the heavy lifting wherever the data is informative.

**Posterior.** A probability distribution over a parameter *after* updating the prior with the observed data, via Bayes' theorem. Summarised by means, medians, and credible intervals.

**Credible interval (HDI).** An interval that contains a specified probability mass of the posterior. We use 90% highest-density intervals (HDIs) throughout. Interpretation: *given the model and data, there is a 90% probability that the true value lies in the interval*. This interpretation is what most people mean by "confidence interval" but it is only valid for Bayesian intervals.

**Prior-predictive distribution.** The distribution over data implied by the prior alone, before any observation. Used in our workflow to sanity-check that the priors generate plausible age-vocabulary curves before fitting.

**Posterior-predictive distribution.** The distribution over future data implied by the posterior. Used to check that the fitted model can reproduce the observed data and to make probabilistic statements about new observations.

**Population-level prediction.** A prediction at $\delta = 0$ for every random effect — i.e., the conditional distribution at a "typical" study and "typical" subject. Used for the trajectory tables and curves in this report.

**Subject-marginal prediction.** A prediction that integrates over the subject random-effect prior. The correct distribution to use for predictive intervals around an *unseen* DS child's word count. Distinct from the population-level prediction: the latent mean is the same but the predictive spread is wider.

**Effective sample size (ESS).** A measure of how many *effectively independent* posterior draws an MCMC chain has produced. We require ESS_bulk ≥ 400 on every reported parameter; ESS_bulk_min is the minimum across reported parameters for a given model.

**$\hat r$ (R-hat).** The potential-scale-reduction factor — a between-chain agreement statistic. Values close to 1.0 indicate the chains have converged; we require $\hat r \leq 1.01$ on every reported parameter.

**Divergence.** A numerical failure of the leapfrog integrator in HMC sampling, indicating the sampler may have missed a region of the posterior. We monitor divergences and would investigate any sustained pattern; an isolated divergence in an otherwise well-mixed model is treated as sampler noise.

**NUTS / HMC.** The No-U-Turn Sampler — an adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm [@hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014]. Used via `nutpie` and PyMC.

## Model comparison

**LOO / PSIS-LOO.** Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [@vehtariPracticalBayesianModel2017]. Reports the expected log predictive density (elpd) of each model on held-out observations. Reliable for VG01–VG07; unreliable for VG08 and VG09 because of singleton subjects.

**elpd.** Expected log predictive density. Larger (less negative) is better. Differences between models are quoted with their standard error (dSE); differences of $\geq 3 \times \mathrm{dSE}$ are usually treated as statistically significant.

**K-fold leave-one-subject-out (LOSO).** A cross-validation procedure in which subjects (not individual observations) are partitioned into $K$ folds; each fold is held out, the model is refit on the remaining folds, and the marginal predictive log-density is computed on the held-out subjects with their random effects drawn from the prior. The gold standard for ranking the random-intercept models in this report; ranks VG09 > VG08 > VG07.

**Conditional LOSO.** A simpler version that holds each subject's random effect at its posterior estimate, so the predictive density is conditioned on having seen that subject's own data. Biased toward more flexible models; useful for "given that we have observations on these children, which model fits them best".

**Marginal LOSO.** Integrates the subject random effect over its prior via Monte Carlo. Mathematically equivalent to conditional LOSO for models without subject REs, but our 12 May 2026 marginal LOSO computation gave very different answers because of PSIS instability on a thinned posterior. The marginal numbers are kept for transparency but should not be used.

## Project-specific terminology

**`rep` configuration.** The sampling configuration used for all reported quantities: 6 chains × 6 000 tuning + 6 000 draw NUTS steps with `target_accept = 0.95`.

**`dev` and `test` configurations.** Smaller sampling configurations used for development and for the K-fold LOSO refits. Results from these are not cited in this report unless explicitly noted.

**Leftward hook.** The non-monotonic appearance of the median understood-vs-spoken trajectory in VG05, in which the understood coordinate retreats between roughly 40 and 60 months while the spoken coordinate continues to rise. A Simpson's-paradox artefact resolved by VG07; see the [Simpson's paradox section of the model comparison chapter](model-comparison.qmd#sec-simpsons-paradox).

**Simpson's paradox.** A statistical phenomenon in which an aggregate trend across a pooled dataset reverses or differs from the trend within each subgroup. Here: within each contributing study, words understood increases with age, but pooled across studies (with the mix changing systematically with age), it appears to dip between 40 and 60 months.
